title: MATH GAOKAO - 424
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.concept: Necessary and Sufficient Conditions in Divisibility
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether one condition is necessary or sufficient for another in a divisibility context.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the condition "\(n\) is divisible by \(3\)" and \(q\) be the condition "\(n\) is divisible by \(6\)" for an integer \(n\). Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: \(p\) is a sufficient condition for \(q\), but not a necessary condition.

options.label: B
options.text: \(p\) is a necessary condition for \(q\), but not a sufficient condition.

questions.explanation: If \(q\) is true, then \(n\) is divisible by \(6\). Since \(6=2\cdot 3\), this implies \(n\) is divisible by \(3\), so \(p\) is true. Hence \(p\) is necessary for \(q\). However, \(n=3\) satisfies \(p\) but does not satisfy \(q\), so \(p\) is not sufficient for \(q\). Therefore, \(p\) is necessary but not sufficient for \(q\).
questions.hint: Recall that \(p\) is sufficient for \(q\) when \(p\Rightarrow q\), and \(p\) is necessary for \(q\) when \(q\Rightarrow p\).

questions.learningObjective: Identify a condition that is sufficient but not necessary for a given property.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the condition "\(n\) is divisible by \(4\)" and \(q\) be the condition "\(n\) is even" for an integer \(n\). Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: \(p\) is a sufficient condition for \(q\), but not a necessary condition.

options.label: B
options.text: \(p\) is a necessary condition for \(q\), but not a sufficient condition.

questions.explanation: If \(n\) is divisible by \(4\), then \(n=4k\) for some integer \(k\), so \(n=2(2k)\) is even. Thus \(p\Rightarrow q\), so \(p\) is sufficient for \(q\). However, \(n=2\) is even but not divisible by \(4\), so \(q\) does not imply \(p\). Hence \(p\) is not necessary for \(q\). Therefore, \(p\) is sufficient but not necessary for \(q\).
questions.hint: Test whether the first condition always forces the second, and whether the second can occur without the first.

questions.concept: Necessary and Sufficient Conditions for Inequalities
questions.learningObjective: Determine the logical relationship between two inequality conditions.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the condition "\(x>0\)" and \(q\) be the condition "\(x>5\)" for a real number \(x\). Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: \(p\) is a sufficient condition for \(q\), but not a necessary condition.

options.label: B
options.text: \(p\) is a necessary condition for \(q\), but not a sufficient condition.

questions.explanation: If \(x>5\), then certainly \(x>0\), so \(q\Rightarrow p\). Therefore \(p\) is necessary for \(q\). But \(x=1\) satisfies \(p\) while failing \(q\), so \(p\not\Rightarrow q\). Thus \(p\) is not sufficient for \(q\). Hence \(p\) is necessary but not sufficient for \(q\).
questions.hint: Check which condition is implied by the other, and then look for a counterexample to the reverse implication.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a proposed value is sufficient or necessary for an equation to hold.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the condition "\(x=2\)" and \(q\) be the condition "\(x^2=4\)" for a real number \(x\). Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: \(p\) is a sufficient condition for \(q\), but not a necessary condition.

options.label: B
options.text: \(p\) is a necessary condition for \(q\), but not a sufficient condition.

questions.explanation: If \(x=2\), then \(x^2=2^2=4\), so \(p\Rightarrow q\). Hence \(p\) is sufficient for \(q\). However, \(x=-2\) also satisfies \(x^2=4\), so \(q\) does not imply \(p\). Thus \(p\) is not necessary for \(q\). Therefore, \(p\) is sufficient but not necessary for \(q\).
questions.hint: Consider all real solutions of the equation \(x^2=4\), not only the positive one.

questions.learningObjective: Analyze necessary and sufficient conditions among quadrilateral properties.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the condition "a quadrilateral is a square" and \(q\) be the condition "a quadrilateral is a rectangle." Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: \(p\) is a sufficient condition for \(q\), but not a necessary condition.

options.label: B
options.text: \(p\) is a necessary condition for \(q\), but not a sufficient condition.

questions.explanation: Every square is a rectangle, so \(p\Rightarrow q\). Therefore \(p\) is sufficient for \(q\). However, a rectangle need not be a square, so \(q\not\Rightarrow p\). Thus \(p\) is not necessary for \(q\). Hence \(p\) is sufficient but not necessary for \(q\).
questions.hint: Recall the inclusion relationships among special quadrilaterals such as squares and rectangles.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether one inequality condition is necessary or sufficient for another.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the condition "\(x>1\)" and \(q\) be the condition "\(x>3\)" for a real number \(x\). Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: \(p\) is a sufficient condition for \(q\), but not a necessary condition.

options.label: B
options.text: \(p\) is a necessary condition for \(q\), but not a sufficient condition.

questions.explanation: If \(x>3\), then \(x>1\) automatically, so \(q\Rightarrow p\). Hence \(p\) is necessary for \(q\). However, \(x=2\) satisfies \(p\) but not \(q\), so \(p\not\Rightarrow q\). Thus \(p\) is not sufficient for \(q\). Therefore, \(p\) is necessary but not sufficient for \(q\).
questions.hint: Compare the intervals determined by the two inequalities and check the direction of implication.

questions.learningObjective: Analyze a condition on a product and a condition on one factor.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the condition "\(ab=0\)" and \(q\) be the condition "\(a=0\)" for real numbers \(a\) and \(b\). Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: \(p\) is a sufficient condition for \(q\), but not a necessary condition.

options.label: B
options.text: \(p\) is a necessary condition for \(q\), but not a sufficient condition.

questions.explanation: If \(a=0\), then \(ab=0\cdot b=0\), so \(q\Rightarrow p\). Therefore \(p\) is necessary for \(q\). However, \(ab=0\) can also occur when \(b=0\) and \(a\ne 0\), for example \(a=1,\ b=0\). Thus \(p\not\Rightarrow q\), so \(p\) is not sufficient for \(q\). Hence \(p\) is necessary but not sufficient for \(q\).
questions.hint: Remember that a product of real numbers is zero if at least one factor is zero.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether being equilateral is sufficient or necessary for being isosceles.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the condition "a triangle is equilateral" and \(q\) be the condition "a triangle is isosceles." Which statement is correct? An isosceles triangle is defined here as a triangle with at least two equal sides.

options.label: A
options.text: \(p\) is a sufficient condition for \(q\), but not a necessary condition.

options.label: B
options.text: \(p\) is a necessary condition for \(q\), but not a sufficient condition.

questions.explanation: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal, so it certainly has at least two equal sides. Hence \(p\Rightarrow q\), and \(p\) is sufficient for \(q\). However, an isosceles triangle need not be equilateral, so \(q\not\Rightarrow p\). Thus \(p\) is not necessary for \(q\). Therefore, \(p\) is sufficient but not necessary for \(q\).
questions.hint: Use the definitions of equilateral and isosceles triangles in terms of side lengths.

questions.concept: Sufficient Condition for Monotonicity on an Interval
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a specific interval is sufficient or necessary for a function to be increasing.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the condition "\(I=[1,2]\)" and \(q\) be the condition "the function \(f(x)=x^2\) is increasing on the interval \(I\)." Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: \(p\) is a sufficient condition for \(q\), but not a necessary condition.

options.label: B
options.text: \(p\) is a necessary condition for \(q\), but not a sufficient condition.

questions.explanation: On the interval \([1,2]\), if \(x_1<x_2\), then \(x_1^2<x_2^2\) because both numbers are nonnegative and increasing. Thus \(p\Rightarrow q\), so \(p\) is sufficient for \(q\). However, \(f(x)=x^2\) is also increasing on other intervals such as \([0,1]\), so \(q\) does not require \(I=[1,2]\). Hence \(p\) is not necessary for \(q\). Therefore, \(p\) is sufficient but not necessary for \(q\).
questions.hint: Check whether the chosen interval guarantees increasing behavior, and then ask whether other intervals could also work.

questions.concept: Sufficient Condition for Convergence of a Sequence
questions.learningObjective: Analyze necessary and sufficient conditions for convergence of a real sequence.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the condition "the real sequence \(\{a_n\}\) is bounded and monotonic" and \(q\) be the condition "the real sequence \(\{a_n\}\) converges." Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: \(p\) is a sufficient condition for \(q\), but not a necessary condition.

options.label: B
options.text: \(p\) is a necessary condition for \(q\), but not a sufficient condition.

questions.explanation: By the monotone convergence theorem, every bounded monotonic real sequence converges. Hence \(p\Rightarrow q\), so \(p\) is sufficient for \(q\). However, a convergent sequence need not be monotonic; for example, \(a_n=\frac{(-1)^n}{n}\) converges to \(0\) but is not monotonic. Thus \(q\not\Rightarrow p\), so \(p\) is not necessary for \(q\). Therefore, \(p\) is sufficient but not necessary for \(q\).
questions.hint: Recall the monotone convergence theorem and consider a convergent sequence that oscillates while approaching its limit.
